en: Did they scatter his four kinds of livestock?
Bereft of my generous lord,
Has God truly struck us?
Utterly bereft of our precious one,
Are the forty companions left desolate?
A battle-axe with a hawthorn shaft—
Who will fit it so it does not twist?
The teeming people, Kyrgyz and many Argyn—
Who will lead them without letting them scatter?
A battle-axe with a black blade—
Who will fit it so it does not wobble?
And the countless Nogai and Kyrgyz
Who will lead them without bringing sorrow?
To his right are the Russians,
On the ridge are the Chinese,
Ahead of him are the Franks.
There are many enemies who contend with me.
He was a man without care,
A lion born a leopard.
If You, God, cherish his life,
God, keep Manas safe!
Have enemies come from Mecca,
With grievous, insatiable claims,
And utterly destroyed me?
Plunging all our dark eyes into grief,
Have they killed him and gone?
Where even the Flood had never swept—
Against my valiant lord
Beijing had a claim.
Perhaps it has overwhelmed my hero,
Perhaps the smiting God has struck him,
Perhaps left him like an extinguished fire.
On his right were the Russian people.
From moon-bright Sary-Talaa,
Sixty Russian surveyors,
Wearing their yellow coats,
All on matching bay mares,
All rode bareback.
The sixty Russians from afar
Fled in a noisy rush.
Almambet and Bakai, the two khans,
Out on the open steppe,
Killed the Russian surveyors.
Khan Manas's great spyglass
They seized from them as plunder.
The Russians too have vengeance to take.
Ruin-bringing, gray-maned Manas—
Have the Russians slaughtered him?
When I think of it, my fate is dark.
Have they utterly destroyed me?”
“Manas! Manas!” he shouted,
Calling, unable to find Kanykei,
Darkened with grief,
Bereft of his sultan, Khan Manas,
Roaring without cease,
He came to the site of the stronghold.
There was freshly dug earth there,
And a track for a single horse.
Where Akayar had been imprisoned,
There was the pit of the five mighty warriors.
Roaring at the edge of the pit,
Kyrgylchal stood above it,
Calling out for Akayar.
With life barely in him,
With his strength nearly gone,
Akayar lay there.
Thirty days had passed,
And his plight had grown terrible.
Wounded in eighteen places,
His whole body in dreadful condition,
Drenched in blood,
As though about to die,
He leaned against the bottom of the pit.
For throwing a noose over an untamed horse,
Kyrgylchal had at his side,
For catching horses,
A horsehair rope eighty fathoms long.
He untied it from his side
And flung it down into the pit.
Akayar at the bottom of the pit—
Before a word could be uttered,
In the blink of an eye,
The resourceful Kyrgylchal
Drew him up out of the pit.
How weak Akayar had become,
The keen Kyrgylchal saw.
Red liquor and sweet food,
Kyrgylchal poured, tilting the vessel,
And gave it to Akayar.
Rekindling his extinguished fire,
Of the Ayar who had lain in the pit,
He revived his dying life.
While Kyrgylchal watched him,
What he knew and had learned,
All that had happened, all he had seen,
Hovering between life and death,
The humiliation at the five Kalmyks' hands
That your valiant Manas had suffered,
How they fought but could not prevail
And endured torment together,
How your noble mother's breast
Had been torn by Kozkaman's shot,
How she staggered, beside herself,
How she hurried, at her wits' end,
Laid the generous lord across her saddle,
Lashed Ak-kula with her whip,
And your noble mother Kanykei
Fled toward Mecca—
Akayar told it all.
His eyes closed, his body drooping,
Unholy people who open their arms.
How between life and death
He had remained, Akayar told.
How piercing cries and wild battle-shouts
Had been raised, Akayar told.
Leaving out not a single thing,
Akayar told what he had seen.
How, pretending it was liquor, they gave poison,
The humiliation heaped upon Khan Manas,
Akayar told how they had inflicted it.
How Kanykei escaped and fled,
Carrying the prince across her saddle,
And departed, Akayar told.
His mount had been the tulpar Ker-toru.
How he lost Ker-toru
And was left there, Akayar told.
How the five mighty warriors seized him
And cast him into the pit, Akayar told.
How they wrecked the treasury
And scattered it, Akayar told.
Loading the gold upon their mules,
They had fled, Akayar told him.
Hearing this, Kyrgylchal
Grew terribly agitated.
The forty companions were playing games.
At the forty companions, Kyrgylchal
Shouted in his fury.
He came to the forty companions
Of the companions at play,
He saw their amusement.
In merriment and games
At that moment the forty companions
Were utterly absorbed.
They had drawn an ordo circle forty foot-lengths across
And were playing the game.
Forty young unfoaled mares
They had staked as prizes.
The winners slaughtered their winnings.
When bored, they played ordo;
When not bored, the forty companions
Played freely at their ease.
Shouting, Kyrgylchal
Threw the forty companions into confusion.
Through the great game of the khan's stronghold
He rode, trampling it:
“Golden forelock, tasselled belt—
Is Almambet here?
Piercing cry, wild battle-shout—
Is Chubak here?
He who sets the whole world in uproar—
Is Chunak here?
The saintly old warrior Bakai,
Renowned as the Hungry Lion—
Is that valiant one here?
Azhybai, khan of the Argyn,
With his forked beard and bare chest,
Sart-like face and sunken eyes—
Is that khan here?
Light on a horse, fit even for a colt,
Sleepless, watchful on the road,
A sharp edge of black steel,
Khan Manas's Syrgak,
Who throws the whole world into confusion—
Damn you, bold fellow!
His strength reaches across the world.
He and the generous lord
Are sons of two brothers.
Yraman's Yrchy-uul,
Brave Shuutu, with a hat like a yurt's felt covering!
Damn you, forty companions!
Have you seen what I have seen?
Do you know what I know?
Have you heard what I have heard?
Have you heard news of the fierce lord?
Damn you, forty mighty ones!
Have you killed your enemy
And satisfied your craving for revenge?
Damn you, forty companions!
You were forty dogs from forty different places.
Your horses grew fat and you grew comfortable.
You came from many places and became forty.
You came and settled in Talas,
Became companions to Zhakyp's
Only son, Manas.
One of you came without a horse.
To that horseless companion
A wild sheep's legs, bronze forelegs—
He gave a tulpar to ride.
One of you came without a coat.
That coatless companion
With a golden collar and bronze sleeves,
Double-linked, with rings like a lark's eye—
He clothed him in bulletproof mail.
One of you came without a home.
That homeless companion
With a golden roof-ring and bronze ties,
Which no one entering would wish to leave—
He housed him in a white palace.
One of you came without livestock.
To that stockless companion,
Nine great herds of mountain horses,
Thoroughbreds and swift steeds together,
Brave Manas gave as your allotted share.
One of you came without a wife.
Thimble mouths and eyes like a camel calf's,
Glistening eyes that cast sidelong glances,
Crimson dresses and slender waists—
From among the graceful beauties,
He gave you daughters of the Kyrgyz.
Khan Manas provided you with wives.
One of you came without faith.
To that faithless companion,
With a white turban like a cauldron,
Whose shout rang like the call to prayer,
Khan Manas gave a mullah.
He set you walking on the right path.
The companion who came without faith
He taught God's existence and oneness.
Damn you, forty companions!
Drink stones instead of liquor!
If that is not enough,
Drink your father's blood with them!
Drink the oil of your fish!
Damn you, forty companions!
Rather than all lying about at play,
Drink your mother's blood!
Damn you, forty mighty ones!
You play ordo heedlessly.
Of the sovereign Sultan Manas
Today you will suffer the calamity.
Consider it well, forty companions:
If the warrior Manas is no longer here,
You will have endless tales of grievance;
You have your crooked dealings.
If that mighty one's eyes are gone,
Many lands have vengeance to take.
Unless you flee in all directions,
Forty companions, they may slaughter you all.
If you lose Khan Manas,
Forty companions, you have no garden planted in Ken-Kol,
No time to lie at ease and stretch yourselves.
You have no garden established in Talas,
No time to sprawl at your ease.
Whole otter pelts,
Cutting them apart,
Having them sewn onto your trouser legs—
